open-question.question: In what form does the rendered Antigravity tree name the global plugin root in every path it reads and every python3 command it runs — a tilde path (~/.gemini/config/plugins/cairn), a $HOME-prefixed path, the ${PLUGIN_ROOT} string the agy binary carries for MCP and hook configuration, or a prose rule telling the runner to resolve the root from the absolute SKILL.md path the host loads a skill from — given that the one literal must resolve both in the host's file-reading tool and in a shell command, in the orchestrator and in a dispatched agent whose prompt carries no plugin path?

How does the enable_write_tools: true frontmatter key reach the two rendered Antigravity agent files — written into core/agents/*.md and stripped from the Claude Code and Codex trees through their strip_frontmatter_keys as color is today, added at render time by a new per-host build setting that inserts frontmatter keys, or written into the core files and left standing in every host's tree as a key the other hosts ignore?

Does scripts/build_hosts.py gain a check that fails --check when a rendered Antigravity agent file lacks enable_write_tools: true, so a later edit that drops the key is caught by the drift gate and CI, or is the on-demand agy suite the only guard against the key going missing?
open-question.alternative: scripts/build_hosts.py gains no check and no test is added: the build's check set stays as it is (dangling-plugin-root, foreign-plugin-root, stripped-key-present, frontmatter-missing/invalid/keys, unfilled-placeholder), and the on-demand agy suite's subagent write/shell probe is the only mechanical guard against a rendered Antigravity agent file losing enable_write_tools: true, with code review as the everyday guard. Adds nothing to the build, its settings key set, or the default pytest and CI runs. The guard sits on the observable behaviour (the agent actually writing and running commands), not on a key name, so it also catches the host renaming or reinterpreting the key, which no static check can. The suite runs only on request or when the integration changes, never in CI, so an edit that drops the key (a frontmatter cleanup in core/agents, a strip-list or setting change) passes --check and CI green and ships unnoticed until someone runs agy. That is the exact failure this milestone fixes, where all 11 dispatched subagents ended FAILED:. How easily the key can go missing depends on the sibling Write-tools key mechanism question.

Every host definition gains one new settings key, kept in the shared key set and left empty where a host has nothing to declare, naming the frontmatter keys and values each rendered agent file must carry (Antigravity: enable_write_tools = true; Claude Code and Codex: empty). check_host_tree gains a generic check, for example required-key-missing, that fails --check, and so the drift gate and CI, when a rendered agent lacks a declared key or carries a different value. The agy suite stays as the behavioural check beside it. A dropped key fails the drift gate and CI the moment it is committed, at no runtime cost. The check is host-neutral data plus generic Python, so it keeps the rule that adding a host means adding a definition directory with no host-specific Python, mirrors the existing stripped-key-present check, and serves any later host whose agents need a key. Adds a settings key every definition must declare and one more check to build_hosts.py and its documentation, for what is today a single key on one host. It checks the key only by name and value, so a host-side rename or change in meaning still reaches only the agy suite. If the sibling Write-tools key mechanism question settles on a per-host setting that inserts the key at render time, this check partly re-asserts the build's own output.

scripts/build_hosts.py gains a check written for this one case: when rendering the Antigravity tree, it fails --check, and so the drift gate and CI, if either rendered agent file's frontmatter lacks enable_write_tools: true. The host name and the key are written in the Python, and no settings key is added. The agy suite stays beside it. The smallest change that still puts the guard in --check and CI. One conditional and no new settings key or schema entry for the other definitions to declare. Puts host-specific Python into a build whose recorded rule is that no host-specific Python exists and adding a host means only adding a definition directory. It sets a precedent for per-host special cases in the generic gate and does nothing for a later host with the same need.

The build is unchanged. A test module under tests/ reads the committed hosts/antigravity/agents/*.md frontmatter and fails unless each file carries enable_write_tools: true. It runs in both default pytest runs, so CI catches a dropped key, since --check already forces the committed tree to match a fresh build. The agy suite stays beside it. Catches a dropped key in every CI run with no change to build_hosts.py, its check set, or any host definition's settings key set, so the build stays generic. Puts a host-tree assertion into a suite that otherwise tests the tools under core/tools, and hardcodes the host and key in a test instead of the definition's data. It also fails in pytest rather than in --check, so a maintainer running only the build loop finds out later, and it has to parse frontmatter without PyYAML to keep working at the 3.9 floor.

open-question.question: What do the installation docs say to a user whose project still holds a .agents/plugins/cairn/ copy extracted under an earlier release, which the host would discover beside the global copy — an instruction to remove it, a statement that a workspace-local copy is unsupported, or nothing?
open-question.alternative: The README's Antigravity installation section (the template under scripts/hosts/antigravity/ and the root README.md that carries it word for word) gains a short note for projects that extracted cairn under an earlier release: remove the project's .agents/plugins/cairn/ directory, with the literal command to do so and one clause on why (the old copy is discovered beside the global one, and it predates the subagents' write and shell tools). The note says nothing about how the host ranks or merges the two copies. Gives the one concrete action that removes the risk. A stale 1.8.5-or-earlier copy carries the agent files without enable_write_tools, so if the host loads it the user hits exactly the reported failure again. A command they can paste closes that off without needing to know how the host chooses between duplicates. Puts a destructive command in the install docs that every new reader sees, even though it only applies to projects that installed before this release. It also tells users to act on behaviour nobody has checked: how agy handles two plugins both named cairn, one global and one in .agents/plugins/, was not part of any hands-on check.

The README's Antigravity installation section states that the global ~/.gemini/config/plugins/cairn copy is the only supported installation and that a workspace-local .agents/plugins/cairn/ copy is unsupported. It gives no command and no removal instruction, and says nothing about how the host treats the two copies together. Draws the support line in one declarative sentence that stays true however agy ranks duplicate plugins. Bug reports from a project that still holds an old copy can be pointed back at that sentence, and the docs gain no destructive command. Leaves the user to work out that "unsupported" means "delete it", and that the old copy may be why subagents fail. Someone who skims past it can keep running a copy without write tools, see the reported FAILED: subagents, and get no hint of the cause.

This milestone first checks by hand what agy 1.4.0 does when a workspace holds a .agents/plugins/cairn/ copy beside the global one: whether it loads both, prefers one, or reports a conflict through agy plugin list. The README's Antigravity section then states the observed result and the action that follows from it, which is a removal instruction if the workspace copy is loaded or shadows the global one, and no note if the host ignores it. Bases the docs on what the host actually does rather than on an assumed conflict. The note is written only when it is needed, and when it is, it can say exactly what the user will see, so it holds no guess about precedence and no warning against a problem that doesn't exist. Adds one more hands-on probe to the milestone and makes the README wording depend on its outcome, so the docs task can't be written until the probe has run. The observed behaviour is pinned to one agy version and can drift on a later release without the note being rechecked.

The README's installation section describes only the fresh global install and says nothing about earlier copies. The advice to remove a project's .agents/plugins/cairn/ copy goes into the CHANGELOG.md entry for the release that moves the path, which /release-plugin writes at release time, so it reaches the people who are upgrading. Puts the migration advice where upgrading users look and keeps the install section clean for the far larger set of new readers. Once the release is old, the advice sits in history instead of lingering as a permanent caveat in the README. The milestone itself writes nothing, so whether the advice lands depends on the release step picking it up from the milestone's commits. A user who reinstalls from the README months later without reading the changelog never sees it.

The installation docs say nothing about workspace-local copies, now or later. The Antigravity section shows only the global extract command, and a project that still holds a .agents/plugins/cairn/ copy is left as it is. Keeps the docs to the one install path and adds no wording that depends on unverified host behaviour. The Antigravity tree has had few installs, so few projects, perhaps only the maintainer's own, are likely to hold an old copy at all. Any project that does hold an old copy is left exposed to the exact failure this milestone fixes: the host may load the stale agents, which lack enable_write_tools, and nothing in the docs points to the leftover directory as the cause.

open-question.question: Does the README's Antigravity installation section, now extracting into ~/.gemini/config/plugins/cairn once per machine rather than once per project, tell the user that the host discovers a new plugin directory only on startup and that a running agy session must be restarted after the extract, or does it keep to the extract command alone?
open-question.alternative: The Antigravity installation section in both the README template (scripts/hosts/antigravity/README.md) and the root README.md gets only the new global target: a mkdir -p and the curl | tar extract into ~/.gemini/config/plugins/cairn, with the template's existing paragraph on pinning a release by tag kept. Nothing is said about startup discovery or restarting a running agy session, for a first install or for an update. The section stays parallel to the Claude Code and Codex sections, which carry no restart or reload note, and the README states nothing about host behaviour beyond what the extract does, so there is no sentence to go stale if a later agy release starts discovering plugins while running. The CLI's own plugin guide says a new plugin directory is discovered only on startup, so a user who extracts while an agy session is open finds no /cairn: skills there and has no hint why. The move to a once-per-machine install makes that more likely, since the user is now installing outside any one project's session.

Both the README template and the root README.md follow the extract command with one sentence: Antigravity discovers a new plugin directory only on startup, so restart any agy session that was running during the extract. The note covers the first install only and says nothing about re-extracting a newer release over an existing global copy. It states exactly what agy's built-in plugin guide documents, a new directory found only on startup, and nothing more. One sentence heads off the likeliest first-run failure (cairn missing from the session that is already open) without claiming any unverified behaviour. It says nothing about updates. Whether skills changed by re-extracting over an existing ~/.gemini/config/plugins/cairn take effect in a running session is not documented or verified, so a user updating mid-session may still run stale skill text. It also adds a host-behaviour claim to the README that has to be kept true if agy changes.

Both the README template and the root README.md follow the extract command with a note covering every extract: restart any running agy session after installing, and again after re-extracting a newer or pinned release over the global copy, because the host reads the plugin's directory and skills at startup. One rule covers both the first install and every update, including the tag-pinning path the template already describes. A user never runs a session that mixes the old skill text with the new tool files. The update half goes beyond what the host documents, which is that a new directory is discovered only on startup. Unless this milestone's hands-on check confirms it, the README asserts reload behaviour nobody has verified, and the restart it asks for after an update may be unnecessary.

Both the README template and the root README.md follow the extract command with the first-install restart sentence (a new plugin directory is discovered only on startup, so restart a running agy session) plus a verification command, agy plugin list, which should show cairn enabled at ~/.gemini/config/plugins/cairn. Updates are not addressed. The user can confirm that the global copy landed where the host looks, which is the exact failure the milestone fixes, the orchestrator not finding the plugin at the path it expected. And the restart sentence covers the one case where the copy is in place but the open session cannot see it. It adds a second command and ties the README to the agy plugin list output and its subcommand name, which no other host's section does and which a CLI change can make wrong. A listing shows the plugin is installed, not that the running session has loaded it, so the restart sentence is still what fixes the open-session case.

alternative.id: Restart note in host README only

open-question.alternative: The first-install restart sentence follows the extract command only in the README template, which renders into the cairn-antigravity distribution repository's landing page. The root README.md's Antigravity section keeps to the extract command into ~/.gemini/config/plugins/cairn alone. The root README stays a terse install index whose host sections all have the same shape, and the host-specific detail lives on the page an Antigravity user lands on when installing from that host's distribution repository. The two sections, which today carry the same install command, drift apart, and a user who installs from the root README, the project's main landing page, never sees the note. Keeping two copies of one section in lockstep becomes a judgment call rather than a copy.

open-question.question: Does the milestone correct the sentence in docs/ways-of-using-cairn.md stating that an agy run loads the plugin from its working directory, which the global install makes false, or is the documentation change limited to the README's Antigravity installation section and the host definition's own comments?
open-question.alternative: The documentation change stays limited to the Antigravity installation section of the root README.md and of the scripts/hosts/antigravity/README.md template, plus the host definition's own comments; the docs/ways-of-using-cairn.md sentence saying an agy run loads the plugin from its working directory is left as it stands, and so is every other tracked mention of the workspace-local path (the bug issue template's manifest location, the distribution README's opening sentence about extraction into a workspace's .agents/plugins/cairn/). Keeps the milestone's documentation diff to the two installation sections the goal names, with nothing outside the install path and host definition to review or keep in step. Ships a release whose own docs contradict it: the headless-chain page tells an agy user the plugin is loaded from the project's working directory, and the bug template and distribution README intro point at a .agents/plugins/cairn path the global install no longer uses, so a user following them looks in the wrong place.

Beyond the two installation sections and the host definition's comments, the milestone rewrites the --add-dir bullet in docs/ways-of-using-cairn.md so it no longer says an agy run loads the plugin from its working directory: the run still takes its working directory as its workspace and works on the project there, while the plugin comes from the global install. Other tracked mentions of the workspace-local path (the bug issue template's manifest location, the distribution README's opening sentence) are left unchanged. Corrects the one statement outside the installation sections that describes how an agy run behaves at runtime, the one a headless-chain user acts on, with a one-sentence edit and no wider sweep. Leaves two other stale references in place: the bug report form still asks Antigravity users for the version at .agents/plugins/cairn/plugin.json, and the published distribution README still says its tree is laid out for extraction into a workspace's .agents/plugins/cairn/, both of which name a path a globally installed user does not have.

The milestone corrects every tracked, non-historical statement that names the workspace-local plugin path or says the plugin loads from the working directory: the two installation sections and the host definition's comments, the --add-dir bullet in docs/ways-of-using-cairn.md, the Antigravity manifest location in .github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/bug.yml (to ~/.gemini/config/plugins/cairn/plugin.json), and the opening sentence of the scripts/hosts/antigravity/README.md template that describes extraction into a workspace's .agents/plugins/cairn/. CHANGELOG.md entries and finished milestones' files stay as written, being records of past releases. Leaves no tracked surface a user reads — headless-chain guide, bug form, distribution landing page — naming a path the release no longer installs to, so the global location is the one place every document points. Widens the milestone's documentation diff to files outside the installation sections, including the issue template and the distribution README intro, each of which must be reworded and reviewed; what the reworded text says about a leftover workspace-local copy depends on the sibling question on stale workspace-local copies.

open-question.question: Where does the on-demand agy suite live and how is it kept out of uv run pytest and the CI job — a marked module under tests/ that a default addopts deselects and an explicit marker selects, a directory outside pytest's testpaths that is run by naming its path, or a standalone script outside pytest invoked directly — given that the default run must stay unchanged on a machine with no agy?

Which plugin copy does the agy suite drive — the copy already installed at ~/.gemini/config/plugins/cairn as it stands, the freshly built hosts/antigravity/ tree that the suite installs over that path before running, or a copy installed under an isolated HOME the suite sets for the agy process so the user's own installation is never touched?

How does the agy suite exercise a subagent's write and shell tools and what signal does it accept as a pass — a full /cairn:provide-alternatives-to-all-open-questions run on a fixture milestone, passing when the alternatives land in open_questions.xml and its commit, or a minimal headless prompt that dispatches the agent directly with a trivial write-and-run task, passing on the agent's final message or a file it lands?

Which surfaces does the suite's plugin-root resolution test cover — the orchestrator's file read of a shared procedure, its python3 tool command, and the same two inside a dispatched agent, or only the tool command — given that the report's failures showed up on both the file read and the command?
open-question.alternative: The resolution test covers all four surfaces in both rendered agents: the orchestrator's file read of a shared procedure and its python3 tool command, and inside each dispatched agent (provide-alternatives-to-open-question and complete-task) its own file read of a shared procedure (alternatives-procedure.md, complete-procedure.md) and its own tool command (open_questions.py, task_list.py), each surface asserted separately. Every place the report saw a path fail is pinned, and each agent's distinct procedure file and tool is exercised, so a literal form that resolves in the shell but not in the host's file-reading tool, or in the orchestrator but not in an agent whose prompt carries no plugin path, fails a named assertion rather than a later run. It is the costliest shape: at least two agent dispatches per run, each a slow headless agy process using model calls, and complete-task needs a fixture task it can complete; how cheaply the agent surfaces can be reached depends on the shape the subagent probe takes and the fixture workspace the suite uses.

The resolution test covers all four surfaces — the orchestrator's file read of a shared procedure and its python3 tool command, and the same two inside one dispatched agent (provide-alternatives-to-open-question, the agent the report observed failing) — and does not dispatch complete-task for resolution. Both failure surfaces are covered in both contexts the report distinguishes, including the agent whose prompt carries no plugin path, at the cost of a single agent dispatch; both agents' rendered literals come from the same plugin_root, so one agent stands in for the other's resolution. complete-task's own read of complete-procedure.md and its task_list.py command go unexercised, so a fault specific to that agent file's rendering or context is caught only by its write-tools probe, if that probe touches those paths; whether it does depends on the shape the subagent probe takes.

The resolution test covers the orchestrator only, on both surfaces: its file read of a shared procedure and its python3 tool command; no dispatched agent's resolution is asserted by this test. It pins both failure modes the report observed in the orchestrator — the view_file stat failure and python's exit 2 — in one headless agy process with no dispatch, keeping the test fast and its pass signal simple. The dispatched agent, whose prompt carries no plugin path and which never sees the absolute SKILL.md path the orchestrator receives, is exactly where a form that relies on that metadata would fail, and this test does not look there; agent-side resolution is then verified only if the subagent probe happens to exercise it, which depends on the shape that probe takes.

The resolution test covers the python3 tool command only, in both contexts: once run by the orchestrator and once run inside a dispatched agent; no file read of a shared procedure is asserted in either. A failed command is loud and mechanically checkable (a non-zero exit and a no-such-file line in the transcript or output), whereas a failed file read may be silently recovered by the model searching for the file, so the test keys on the unambiguous signal while still covering the agent context the orchestrator's metadata does not reach. The host's file-reading tool and the shell resolve paths differently (the shell expands a tilde or $HOME, a file-reading tool may not), so a literal form that passes the command check can still break every shared-procedure read; whether that gap matters depends on the literal form chosen for the plugin root.

The resolution test covers one surface in one context: the orchestrator's python3 tool command; neither file reads nor any dispatched agent is asserted. It is the smallest, fastest, and least flaky test: one headless agy process, no dispatch, and a pass signal (the tool's output or exit status) that needs no transcript inspection. It covers one of the four places the report's failures appeared, leaving the file-read surface and the agent context — the two places a literal form is most likely to resolve differently — to be caught only by a later real run; how much that leaves exposed depends on the literal form chosen for the plugin root.

The suite carries no separate resolution test: plugin-root resolution is treated as verified whenever the end-to-end subagent check passes, since that run cannot succeed unless the orchestrator's and the agent's reads and commands resolved; no surface is asserted on its own. It adds no extra agy process or assertion beyond what the suite already runs, keeping the on-demand suite as short and cheap as possible while still failing when resolution is broken. A failure reports only that the run failed, not which surface or context broke, and a model that recovers from a failed read by searching for the file can pass with a broken literal; whether the end-to-end check touches any given surface at all depends on the shape the subagent probe takes.

open-question.question: In what workspace does the agy suite run each headless agy process — a temporary git repository the suite seeds through the plugin's own tools with a milestone and open questions, a committed fixture directory under tests/fixtures/ copied to a temporary location, or the cairn repository checkout itself?

Does the agy suite pin the model, effort, and print timeout it passes on each agy -p line, or run at the host's defaults with no --model, --effort, or --print-timeout as the headless chains in docs/ways-of-using-cairn.md do?

When the agy suite is invoked on a machine where agy is not on PATH or the global plugin copy it needs is absent, does it skip its tests, fail them, or stop before any test with one line naming the missing prerequisite?

How is the goal's rule that the agy suite runs when the Antigravity host integration changes realized, with CI ruled out — a CONTRIBUTING.md sentence naming the paths whose change requires a run before committing, a pre-flight step in the release-plugin skill, or both?

What becomes of the dated hands-on-check block in the header of scripts/hosts/antigravity/settings.toml once a repeatable suite exists — this milestone's run updates it to name agy 1.4.0, the global path, and the write-tools check and it stays the one record of what was checked, or it is replaced by a pointer to the suite as the way to re-check?
